source.title_on_document: The Creative Link Between Words and Ideas is Weakening in the AI Era

paper_design_summary: The core evidence is four preregistered 'natural experiments' that compare college admissions personal statements submitted before (2018-2022) and after (2024-2025) ChatGPT's release at four U.S. institutions, scoring each essay on word-level diversity (DSI), within-essay sentence-level diversity, and document-level distinctness (nearest-neighbor embedding distance to other essays in the same cycle), plus creativity ratings from a GPT-4.1-mini model fine-tuned on expert ratings. Supporting studies compare 1,500 human essays with 1,500 GPT-5-mini essays (correlations among the metrics), regress 22 experts' creativity ratings of 370 pre-ChatGPT essays on the metrics, vary the number of reference essays given to LLM raters (model-only), and run a within-person study in which 203 students uploaded their original admissions essays and wrote prompts that the researchers fed to GPT-4.1 to produce an AI-revised and an AI-generated essay; there is no random assignment in any study.

task.description: College admissions personal statement: 'Please submit a brief essay, either personal or creative, which you feel best describes you.' Mean length about 622 words.

outcomes.name: Document-level distinctness
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Minimum pairwise cosine distance between an essay's OpenAI text-embedding-3-large document embedding and all other essays in the same admissions cycle (higher = more distinct). Scores standardized within institution and level using pooled cycles. Robustness: full unbalanced sample d = -0.16 [-0.18, -0.15] (Table S6, PDF p. 46); with controls for word count, sentence count, sex, race, ethnicity, international status, English at home, Post-ChatGPT beta = -0.16 [-0.18, -0.14] (Table S12a, PDF p. 64); event-time and COVID-period models in Tables S10a and S11a (PDF pp. 55, 59); subgroup models Table S13a, S13e.

contrasts.reported: Post-ChatGPT -0.10 (0.97) vs Pre-ChatGPT 0.05 (1.01) (standardized z, mean (SD)); t = -19.05, df = 49240.59; Cohen's d = -0.15 [-0.17, -0.13]; p < .001; n pre = 47,520, post = 23,760
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 52 (SM p. 26), Table S9; PDF p. 8, Fig. 1

diversity_detail.metric: Document-level Distinctness: minimum pairwise cosine distance to the nearest other essay (Cox et al.)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each essay against all other essays in the same admissions cycle at the same institution (nearest neighbor); cycle sizes equalized by random sampling to 11,880
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Welch's t-test on essay-level standardized scores; Cohen's d with 95% CI
diversity_detail.notes: Higher value = more distinct (more diverse), so no sign reversal. Essay-level test treats essays as independent.

outcomes.name: Sentence-level diversity (within essay)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean pairwise cosine distance between sentence embeddings (SBERT all-MiniLM-L6-v2) within each essay; captures local variation of ideas within one text. Standardized within institution. Robustness: full sample d = -0.09 [-0.10, -0.07] (Table S6); with controls beta = -0.12 [-0.13, -0.10] (Table S12a).

contrasts.locator: PDF p. 52 (SM p. 26), Table S9; PDF p. 8, Fig. 1

outcomes.name: Word-level diversity (Divergent Semantic Integration, DSI)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: DSI: average semantic distance between all word pairs within an essay using BERT (bert-large-uncased, layers 6 and 7) embeddings; an established automated creativity score that the paper treats as surface-level lexical/semantic diversity of one text. Robustness: full sample d = 0.20 [0.18, 0.21] (Table S6); with controls beta = 0.23 [0.21, 0.24] (Table S12a); event-time shows a pre-existing upward trend (Table S10a, Fig. S2).

contrasts.locator: PDF p. 52 (SM p. 26), Table S9; PDF p. 8, Fig. 1

outcomes.name: Creativity rating by expert-tuned GPT-4.1-mini
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Percentile creativity score from GPT-4.1-mini fine-tuned on 22 creativity experts' ratings of 370 pre-ChatGPT essays (held-out r = .82 with expert ratings, Table 1). Reported as the total effect of the post-ChatGPT indicator in a parallel mediation model with word, sentence, and document metrics as mediators (standardized). Direct effect 0.08 [0.07, 0.09]; indirect via word 0.13 [0.13, 0.14]. Table S8 lists this hypothesis as exploratory for EP.

contrasts.reported: Total effect beta = 0.20, 95% CI [0.18, 0.22], p < .001; N = 71,268 essays; bootstrapped with 5,000 resamples
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 85 (SM p. 59), Table S15; PDF p. 14 main text; PDF p. 15, Fig. 3

studies.label: Controlled Experiment 3: within-person original vs AI-revised vs AI-generated essays (203 students)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was randomized. Every participant contributed all three conditions: (1) the original admissions essay they had submitted (written earlier, without AI per the main text), (2) an AI-revised version produced by GPT-4.1 from the original essay plus the participant's revision prompt, and (3) an AI-generated essay produced by GPT-4.1 from the participant's generation prompt. Participants wrote the generation prompt first and the revision prompt second (fixed order); researchers ran the prompts after data collection.
assignment.quote: This procedure resulted in a final dataset where each participant was associated with three distinct essays, allowing us to assess within-person effects of AI use.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 88 (SM p. 62), Controlled Experiment 3; procedure order PDF pp. 86-87 (SM pp. 60-61)

diversity_detail.uncertainty: Linear mixed-effects model with a random intercept per participant; Holm-corrected post-hoc pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means; 95% CIs
diversity_detail.notes: Higher = more distinct; AI conditions lower = more homogeneous across participants. No sign reversal needed.

eligibility.reason: No study randomly assigns people to AI assistance. The four natural experiments (S1-S4) and the pilot (S5) compare essays before and after ChatGPT's release with no observed AI use (observational). Controlled Experiment 3 (S9, 203 people analyzed, PDF p. 86) is a within-person comparison in which every participant contributes an original, an AI-revised, and an AI-generated essay; nothing is randomized, the prompt order is fixed, and the original essays were written years earlier, so it is quasi_people (folded into observational). S6 is AI vs human output and S8 is model-only. Criterion 2 is met only in S9 (203); criterion 3 is met because diversity and creativity are computed on the essays.

one_line_finding: Across four before-after admissions-essay datasets, post-ChatGPT essays had higher word-level diversity (d = 0.15 to 0.39) but lower sentence-level diversity (d = -0.18 to -0.06) and document-level distinctness (d = -0.15 to -0.07) (PDF p. 7 and Fig. 1, p. 8; Table S9, p. 52), and in a non-randomized within-person study of 203 students AI-revised and AI-generated versions were less distinct than the originals (diff = -0.98 and -1.52, PDF p. 16).
open_questions: Main text (PDF p. 16) says participants' original essays were all written 'prior to 2022', but the supplement (PDF p. 86) says 72 sophomores applied during the transitional period and 31 freshmen applied after ChatGPT, so some 'original' essays may have been written when ChatGPT was available.
ChatGPT release date is given as November 30, 2022 (PDF p. 32) and as November 22, 2022 (footnote 1, PDF p. 32).
Table S6 note (PDF p. 46) says all full-sample Welch tests were significant (p < .001), but the selective liberal-arts sentence-level row shows d = -0.02 [-0.04, 0.00], t = -1.67.
Fig. S4 (PDF p. 84) labels the base model 'Base GPT-5.1-mini' while the text says base GPT-5-mini.
The abstract's 372,793 statements equals the four analytic samples including the excluded 2023 cycle (83,160 + 82,975 + 185,580 + 21,078); the main contrasts use 313,388 essays.
For Controlled Experiment 3, the paper does not state which essays form the comparison cohort for document-level distinctness.
Whether the creativity-rating outcome counts as preregistered primary: Table S8 marks the mediation hypothesis 'Pre' for RP, FP, SL and 'Exp' for EP; I coded it secondary.
notes: PDF pages: main text 1-26; supplement SM page s = PDF page s + 26. Natural-experiment counts are essays/applications, not people, so participant fields are null and essay counts are in n_units. Word-level DSI is coded construct 'other' (within-text lexical-semantic diversity; DSI is an automated creativity score) and sentence-level diversity as 'flexibility' (variation of ideas within one person's text); only document-level distinctness compares different people's outputs. Subgroup heterogeneity (Tables S13a-e, Fig. 2, Fig. S1, Fig. S3), event-time models (Tables S10a-c, Fig. S2), COVID-period models (Tables S11a-d), and the word-document association interaction models (Tables S14b-c) are robustness or heterogeneity variants and are summarized in measure_detail rather than listed as separate outcomes. S8 (model-only) has no outcomes on the three questions: the standardized coefficients of the word, sentence, and document metrics predicting LLM creativity ratings did not change systematically across 0 to 128 reference essays (Fig. S4, PDF p. 84).
